# Blood, acid–base, electrolytes and fluids

[All modules](README.md) · [Known misses](../validation/known-misses.md#blood) · 13 source files, 1952 lines · 42 test files

## Purpose

<!-- hand:purpose -->
The blood model computes the patient's fluid compartments, extracellular electrolytes, acid–base state, oxygen
dissociation, oxygen delivery and lactate, and the laboratory results drawn from them, stepped every 100 ms. It also
hands blood-volume changes to the circulation, lung water to the lungs and potassium and calcium effects to the ECG. A
clinician-educator reads it to see why a fluid, a transfusion, bleeding or a drug moves the pH, the potassium or the
lactate; an embedding developer reads it for the blood state and lab outputs the other modules consume.
<!-- /hand:purpose -->

## Equations in words

<!-- hand:equations -->
- Solutes are held as amounts (mmol), so dilution, infusion and bleeding conserve mass, and concentrations are amount
  over extracellular volume (tables §5b.1–§5b.2; `l2/blood/solutes.ts`).
- The pH is the root of an electroneutrality equation: the strong-ion difference, recomputed every step from Na, K,
  iCa, Mg, Cl, lactate and other anions, equals bicarbonate plus the albumin, phosphate and haemoglobin buffer charges;
  bicarbonate is 0.0307·PCO2·10^(pH − 6.1), and the root is found by bounded bisection in pH 6.5–7.9 (Figge, Mydosh &
  Fencl 1992; Van Slyke; tables §5b.1; `l2/blood/acid-base.ts`).
- Haemoglobin saturation is a Hill curve in PO2/P50; carbon monoxide flattens it and lowers P50, and pH, PCO2, 2,3-DPG
  and temperature each shift P50 multiplicatively (Dash & Bassingthwaighte 2004, 2016; tables §5b.3;
  `l2/blood/odc.ts`).
- Arterial O2 content is 13.4·Hb·SaO2·(1 − COHb − MetHb) + 0.03·PaO2 mL/L and delivery is cardiac output times
  content; O2 consumption holds by rising extraction until delivery falls below a critical value, then becomes
  supply-dependent (Cain 1977; Shibutani 1983; Vincent & De Backer 2013; `l2/blood/oxygen.ts`).
- Lactate is produced from the larger of a global deficit below the critical delivery and a regional splanchnic
  deficit when flow falls short of metabolic need, and is cleared in proportion to hepatic blood flow (tables §5.3;
  `l2/blood/oxygen.ts`); hepatic flow is relative cardiac output times the organ model's splanchnic factor, or,
  without the organ model, the square of relative cardiac output (research/13; `l2/blood/core.ts`,
  `l2/blood/params.ts`).
- What glycolysis can actually make of that deficit is braked by the muscle's own limits (E134, `l2/blood/muscle.ts`):
  by the intracellular pH the rate-limiting enzyme sees — a logistic in pHi (= plasma pH − 0.32, the resting 31P-MRS
  offset) with its half at 6.6 and ~0 by 6.3, read off the phosphofructokinase pH curves of Trivedi & Danforth 1966 at
  the high substrate concentration a maximally driven muscle sits at, and normalised to 1 at the resting pH because the
  lactate yield per mL of deficit was itself measured there — and by a muscle glycogen store (85 mmol glucosyl/kg wet
  weight; no limit above 6.5, refilled at 1.5 mmol/kg/h without carbohydrate), and by the surviving muscle mass.
- What glycolysis CANNOT pay for is unpaid ATP, and that is what injures muscle (E134): the dose of unpaid ATP,
  measured against the resting muscle's own bill and summed with the thermal dose (CEM43 of Sapareto & Dewey 1984),
  gives no necrosis below about 120 dose minutes (muscle survives about three hours of warm ischaemia) and complete
  necrosis by 300. Necrotic muscle hands 100 mmol of potassium per kg to the extracellular pool out of the cells, and
  its creatine kinase, myoglobin and phosphate are kept as state only. Active muscle also leaks potassium with its
  metabolic activity (0.36 mmol/L of the set point per × of the resting VO2 the activity adds, from the femoral-vein
  exercise measurements of Medbø & Sejersted 1990). This is the mechanism that replaced the fitted MH efflux, and it
  is not MH-specific: crush, ischaemia and status epilepticus drive it the same way.
- Wherever lactate ACCUMULATES, bicarbonate buffering releases 22 mL of CO2 per mmol (Beaver, Wasserman & Whipp 1986),
  added to the CO2 load the gas model takes (E131 for the MH muscle's share, E134 for every bed). It follows the NET
  accumulation, not the gross flux: clearing the lactate consumes the proton again, so a lactate at a plateau releases
  none. The anaerobic ATP turnover's heat (98 J per mmol of lactate) goes to the heat model, which adds it to the core
  beside the oxidative heat. The delivered share of the demand (achieved ÷ demanded VO2) is written to the heat model,
  which scales its oxidative heat by it, and so is a skin-perfusion flow fraction, cardiac output ÷
  DO2crit/(13.4·Hb_ref·0.97), for the blood-borne core–skin transfer (`l2/blood/pipeline.ts`).
- Fluid moves between plasma and interstitium by a whole-body Starling relation in capillary pressure, interstitial
  pressure and the colloid osmotic gradient, with a reflection coefficient that falls as capillary leak rises, plus a
  lymph return and an elimination of excess blood volume (Landis–Pappenheimer, after Pulse; fitted to Hahn's
  crystalloid kinetics; tables §5b.4; `l2/blood/fluids.ts`).
- Haematocrit is Hb·3/100 (MCHC 33.3 g/dL), and total body water is 0.6 (male) or 0.5 (female) L/kg of actual weight,
  two-thirds intracellular (`l2/blood/params.ts`).
- Doses the blood model owns (succinylcholine potassium release, insulin–dextrose, salbutamol, calcium, citrate,
  bicarbonate, magnesium) act through closed-form curves of time since the dose (tables §5b.1–§5b.2;
  `l2/blood/treatments.ts`).
- Venous gases for the lab panel take PvCO2 − PaCO2 = VCO2/(Q·S) and invert the dissociation curve for venous PO2
  (`l2/blood/labs.ts`).
<!-- /hand:equations -->

| `SIGMA_LEAK_FLOOR` | `0.3` | — | Rippe & Haraldsson 1994; [ENG] | The protein reflection coefficient of a leaky endothelium. Inflammation opens LARGE pores, which carry most of the extra hydraulic conductance and most of the protein flux (two-pore theory, the DIRECTION: Rippe & Haraldsson 1994 Physiol Rev 74:163). That the non-reflected share (1 − σ) grows with the same factor as the whole Kf is an assumption [ENG]: σ = 1 − (1 − σ0)·kfMult, floor SIGMA_LEAK_FLOOR [ENG]. Normal (kfMult 1) → 0.9; warm septic shock (kfMult 2.6) → 0.74; kfMult 3 → 0.7. It applies to every writer of `fl.kfMult` — the endocrine model's sepsis, anaphylaxis and burns alike. |

| `PFK_PHI_HALF` | `6.6` | — | Chem 1966; LL et al. 1989; [P: the article's Figs 1–2 were read for this change] | The phosphofructokinase pH brake (Trivedi B, Danforth WH, J Biol Chem 1966;241:4110–4114 [P: the article's Figs 1–2 were read for this change]). Frog and mouse muscle extracts at 4 mM ATP: activity goes from ≈ 0 to its plateau over 0.3–0.4 pH units, and the MIDPOINT moves about one pH unit with the fructose-6-phosphate concentration — pH 7.44 at 0.054 mM F6P, 7.0 at 0.11 mM, ≈ 6.6 at 0.434 mM. The high-F6P row is the one that belongs here: a muscle driven to its glycolytic maximum accumulates F6P (the authors' own argument that a loss of F6P affinity does not by itself slow the flux), and the in-vivo floor agrees — whole-muscle 31P-MRS pHi in exercise to intolerance stops falling at 6.6–6.8 [S], which is where the flux has stopped. The width 0.1 is the figures' own steepness. At ATP 0.125 mM the pH sensitivity disappears altogether, so this brake is a property of muscle at physiological (mM) ATP. Expressed on pHi; on the PLASMA pH the half is 6.92 (= 6.6 − PHI_OFFSET), inside the 6.9–7.0 the brief states. KNOWN DEVIATION: phosphorylase is inhibited by H+ as well (Spriet LL et al. 1989) [S] — one brake stands for both. |
| `PFK_PHI_W` | `0.1` | — | — | — |
| `PH_PLASMA_REST` | `7.4` | — | — | Muscle intracellular pH at rest, 31P-MRS of the quadriceps: 7.08 ± 0.03 at a plasma pH of 7.40 [S], i.e. an offset of −0.32. The engine moves pHi with the plasma pH one for one, which is right when the cell is making the acid itself (shock, MH, arrest — every case that reaches this brake) and WRONG for an acid–base change imposed from outside: at rest pHi is defended against a bicarbonate load (blood pH and HCO3 rose, muscle pH did not [S]), and a CO2 load moves pHi the other way. So a bicarbonate dose releases this brake more than it should (known deviation). |
| `GLYCOLYSIS_HEAT_J_PER_MMOL` | `98` | mmol | Rev 1978; Physiol 2000; Physiol 2003; [P: that paper's methods were read for this change; the two older papers are second-hand] | The heat of anaerobic ATP turnover, J per mmol of lactate made from glycogen. The primary quantity is per ATP: 35 kJ/mol for PCr hydrolysis, 65 for glycolysis and 72 for oxidation (Curtin NA, Woledge RC, Physiol Rev 1978;58:690–761; Woledge RC, Reilly PJ, Biophys J 1988;54:97–104), as used with the same 1.5 ATP per lactate by González-Alonso J, Quistorff B, Krustrup P, Bangsbo J, Saltin B, J Physiol 2000;524:603–615 [P: that paper's methods were read for this change; the two older papers are second-hand]. Krustrup P et al., J Physiol 2003;549:255 use 67 and give the published range 65–78 kJ/mol ATP. 65 × 1.5 = 98 J per mmol lactate (the range gives 98–117). DERIVED: no paper states a per-lactate enthalpy. It already includes the proton transfer to the cell's buffers (that is why Woledge & Reilly's PCr value is −35 and not −44 kJ/mol). Di Prampero's O2 equivalent of blood lactate (≈ 3 mL O2/kg per mmol/L) is a DIFFERENT quantity (whole-body, accumulation) and is not used here. |
| `K_ACT_PER_VO2X` | `0.36` | — | Physiol 1990; [P: abstract and the reachable text] | Potassium of ACTIVE muscle: mmol/L of the plasma K set point per × of the resting whole-body VO2 that the muscle's activity adds. Twenty trained men ran one minute to exhaustion with femoral catheters: arterial K peaked at 8.17 ± 0.29 mmol/L and femoral venous at 8.34, from ≈ 4.2 (Medbø JI, Sejersted OM, J Physiol 1990;421:105–122 [P: abstract and the reachable text]); the peak was linearly related to the exercise intensity, though the paper gives no slope. Δ ≈ +4.0 mmol/L at an intensity of about × 12 the resting VO2 → 0.36 per ×. DERIVED, and an UPPER bound: that is a one-minute peak with almost no time for re-uptake, while this term is a steady-state set-point shift (after exercise the same subjects undershot by 0.5 mmol/L on a stimulated pump). It replaces the fitted MH_K_EFFLUX 2.35 mmol/L at activity 1, which was 6.5 × larger because it had to carry the rhabdomyolysis the model did not have. |
| `MUSCLE_K_MMOL_PER_KG` | `100` | kg | [TXT] | Muscle intracellular potassium, mmol per kg wet weight: ICF K ≈ 140 mmol/L of cell water × 0.75 L water/kg [TXT]. |
| `MUSCLE_CK_U_PER_KG` | `2.5e6` | kg | [VERIFY: orders of magnitude] | Muscle creatine kinase, myoglobin and total phosphate per kg wet weight — released by necrosis and kept as STATE only (no display, no effect; the phosphate does not enter the acid–base yet) [VERIFY: orders of magnitude]. |
| `MUSCLE_MB_MG_PER_KG` | `4000` | kg | — | — |
| `MUSCLE_PI_MMOL_PER_KG` | `60` | kg | — | — |
| `MUSCLE_REST_VO2_FRAC` | `0.2` | — | [TXT: ≈ 20 % of resting oxygen uptake at rest] | The muscle's share of the resting VO2 [TXT: ≈ 20 % of resting oxygen uptake at rest] — the clock the injury dose is measured against (one "dose minute" = one minute with the whole resting muscle bill unpaid). |
| `INJ_TOL_DOSE_MIN` | `120` | — | Surg 2002; Surg 1987 | The unpaid-ATP dose at which necrosis begins and at which it is complete, in dose minutes. Warm ischaemia of skeletal muscle: irreversible change after about three hours, severe or complete by six (Blaisdell FW, Cardiovasc Surg 2002;10:620–630; Labbe R, Lindsay T, Walker PM, J Vasc Surg 1987;6:152–157) [S: reviews, not re-read]. The first hour of that is paid for by anaerobic glycolysis, which this model produces on its own, so the dose that is left runs from ≈ 120 to ≈ 300 dose minutes. |
| `INJ_FULL_DOSE_MIN` | `300` | — | — | — |
| `CEM43_R_HOT` | `0.5` | — | Phys 1984; Physiol 1978 | Thermal injury on the same tolerance: the cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C, CEM43 = Σ R^(43−T)·dt with R = 0.5 above 43 °C and 0.25 below (Sapareto SA, Dewey WC, Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 1984;10:787–800) [S]. The threshold CEM43_MUSCLE_MIN is derived from the human critical thermal exposure, 42 °C for about 45 min (Bynum GD et al., Am J Physiol 1978;235:R228) [S]: 45 × 0.25 = 11 CEM43 minutes. Rather than a second damage curve, the thermal dose consumes the SAME tolerance (one insult, two clocks), scaled so that 11 CEM43 minutes alone reach it. |
| `CEM43_R_COLD` | `0.25` | — | — | — |
| `CEM43_MUSCLE_MIN` | `11` | — | — | — |
| `CEM43_FROM_C` | `38` | — | [ENG guard: a febrile 39 °C for two hours is 1.9 CEM43 minutes, well under the threshold, so the guard only removes the meaningless tail] | The dose model is calibrated around 43 °C and says nothing about normothermia, so no thermal dose is counted below this core temperature — otherwise an ordinary 37 °C day would creep toward necrosis [ENG guard: a febrile 39 °C for two hours is 1.9 CEM43 minutes, well under the threshold, so the guard only removes the meaningless tail]. |
